questions.question: How are arrow functions different from regular functions in JavaScript?
questions.title: Arrow Functions vs Regular Functions
questions.direct_answer: Arrow functions are short function expressions that capture `this`, `arguments`, `super`, and `new.target` from the surrounding scope. Regular functions receive call-dependent `this`, have their own `arguments`, and may be constructors, so arrow functions fit callbacks but not every method or constructor.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the semantic differences behind arrow syntax, especially receiver binding and construction.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an arrow as an object method and expecting `this` to become that object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain lexical `this` with one callback example and name the constructor and `arguments` boundaries.

Wrap an implicitly returned object literal in parentheses: `value => ({ value })`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An arrow function is a compact function expression, but its important difference is lexical context. It does not create its own `this`, `arguments`, `super`, or `new.target`; it reads those names from the surrounding scope where the arrow was created. Shorter syntax is useful, but it is not the main semantic rule.

A regular function receives `this` from the way it is called. `account.read()` can set the receiver to `account`, while calling an extracted `read()` loses that method call. `call`, `apply`, and `bind` can provide a receiver to a regular function, but they cannot replace the `this` already captured by an arrow.

An arrow is a good fit for a callback that should keep its surrounding receiver. In the example, the regular method receives the `counter` object as `this`, and the arrow used by `forEach` keeps that same value. A regular callback there would need an explicit receiver, a closure, or `bind`.

Arrow functions cannot be used with `new`, do not provide their own construction `prototype`, and cannot be generator functions. They also have no own `arguments`, so a rest parameter such as `(...values)` is clearer when all inputs are needed. For an implicit object return, wrap the literal as `value => ({ value })`; otherwise the braces are parsed as a block body.

questions.question: How does destructuring work with arrays, objects, defaults, renaming, and rest values?
questions.title: JavaScript Destructuring Patterns
questions.direct_answer: Destructuring matches an array or object against a binding pattern and assigns selected values to names. Array patterns use positions; object patterns use property keys. Defaults apply only when the matched value is `undefined`, renaming changes the local name, and a final rest element collects the remaining values shallowly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can predict bindings, defaults, aliases, rest output, and shallow reference behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting a default to replace `null`, or reading `{ id: userId }` as creating a variable named `id`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate missing or `undefined` from `null` and show that object rest does not deep-clone nested data.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Array destructuring reads iterable values by position; object destructuring reads properties by key.
`const { id: userId } = user` reads property `id` into local name `userId`.
A destructuring default runs for a missing or `undefined` value, but not for `null`.
Array rest creates a new array; object rest copies remaining enumerable own properties into a new object.
Destructuring and rest are shallow, so nested objects can still be shared.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Destructuring is binding syntax that selects values using a pattern. An array pattern reads iterable values by position, so `const [first, second] = values` takes the first two items. An object pattern reads properties by key, so `const { id } = user` selects the property named `id`. The source itself is not changed. The same patterns also work in function parameters and loop headers.

Array patterns can skip a position, and either form can provide defaults or collect remaining values. Object syntax can also rename while reading: in `const { id: userId } = user`, `id` is the source key and `userId` is the local variable. A rest element must be last because it gathers what remains.

A destructuring default is used when the matched value is missing or exactly `undefined`. It does not replace `null`, `false`, `0`, or an empty string. For example, `{ theme: null }` destructured with `{ theme = "light" }` keeps `null`, allowing an API to distinguish an omitted value from a value supplied deliberately.

Array rest creates a new array, while object rest copies the remaining enumerable own properties into a new object. Both operations are shallow. In the example, changing `rest.profile.city` also changes `user.profile.city` because both outer objects still refer to the same nested profile object. Deep ownership needs an intentional deeper copy.

sections.title: Concept: JavaScript Destructuring Patterns
sections.content:
**Mechanism.** A binding pattern contains slots. Array slots consume values from an iterator in order. Object slots perform property access with named keys. The source itself is not mutated by the binding operation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Source user object] -->|id| I[local userId]
  S -->|role is undefined| D[default viewer]
  S -->|remaining own properties| R[new rest object]
  R --> N[nested references remain shared]
```

**Runnable example.** This example covers position, renaming, a default, and rest without hiding the resulting values.

```javascript
const coordinates = [12, 30, 99];
const [x, y, ...extra] = coordinates;

const user = { id: 7, role: undefined, profile: { city: "Pune" } };
const { id: userId, role = "viewer", ...rest } = user;

rest.profile.city = "Goa"; // shallow copy shares profile
console.log(x, y, extra);      // 12 30 [99]
console.log(userId, role);     // 7 viewer
console.log(user.profile.city); // Goa
```

**Boundary.** A rest element must be last. When an existing object binding is reassigned with object destructuring, parentheses are normally required around the assignment so the opening brace is not parsed as a block.

questions.question: Which arrow-function and destructuring mistakes commonly cause JavaScript bugs?
questions.title: Arrow and Destructuring Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: Frequent bugs include using an arrow where a method needs call-dependent `this`, returning an object literal without parentheses, destructuring an absent argument, and assuming rest creates a deep copy. Each failure comes from treating concise syntax as equivalent to the longer form when its binding or ownership rules differ.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can connect common symptoms to the exact arrow, parsing, destructuring, or copy-depth rule.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Replacing concise syntax randomly without identifying whether the bug is receiver binding or missing input.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a symptom-to-rule diagnosis and preserve concise syntax where its contract is correct.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use regular method syntax when the receiver should supply `this`.
Write `item => ({ id: item.id })` to return an object expression implicitly.
Give a destructured parameter an outer default, such as `({ name } = {})`, when omission is allowed.
Spread and rest create shallow containers; nested references are not cloned.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An arrow used as an object method does not receive that object as `this`; it captures `this` from outside. When the method should use its call receiver, write `read() { return this.total; }`. Keep the arrow for an inner callback only when that callback should preserve the method's receiver.

The arrow `item => { id: item.id }` uses a block body and does not return the object. Write `item => ({ id: item.id })` for an implicit object expression, or use a block with an explicit `return`. The parentheses tell the parser that the braces begin an expression.

A property default cannot help when the entire argument is absent. `function label({ name })` throws if called with no argument. When omission is allowed, `function label({ name = "Guest" } = {})` first supplies an object, then supplies the property. An explicit `null` still needs validation because neither default replaces it.

Rest creates a new outer container but keeps references to nested objects. Mutating a nested value through the rest object can therefore change the original source. Copy more deeply only where independent ownership is required. The useful diagnosis is the broken rule—receiver, return syntax, input presence, or copy depth—not a blanket ban on concise syntax.
